title: Pulses and Persistence: How Timing Sets Fate

scenes.visual: Dark slate background (#0F172A), reusing the first film's colour map (teal = responders and repair, amber = restraints, coral = stress triggers and permanent arrest or death). A two-panel live-cell monitor fills 70% of frame height (schematic): four outlined cells glow faintly teal on the left, while an empty time-trace axis sits above a Repair-vs-Arrest fate bar on the right. Title 'Pulses and Persistence: How Timing Sets Fate' appears in crisp white (size 40) and fades out.

scenes.tts: In the first film, removing a restraint let a stress responder climb fast. Once p fifty-three rises, how does a cell choose between repair and permanent arrest? Does heavier damage simply turn p fifty-three up like a dimmer dial? To find out, researchers watched one living cell at a time.

scenes.visual: Same two-panel monitor carried in place. A coral radiation flash strikes the four cells on the left; teal p53 brightens inside them. On the right, a hypothetical white dimmer-dial gauge tilts up with a question mark, then dissolves into a live microscope viewport focusing onto one single cell.

scenes.tts: Grind millions of irradiated cells onto a blot, and p fifty-three rises and fades, at most with a ripple. That dish average looks like a dial. Film single living cells instead, and p fifty-three fires separate pulses of fixed average height and width. Higher doses add more pulses on average, not taller ones.
scenes.caption: Grind millions of irradiated cells onto a blot, and p53 rises and fades, at most with a ripple. That dish average looks like a dial. Film single living cells instead, and p53 fires separate pulses of fixed average height and width. Higher doses add more pulses on average, not taller ones.
scenes.visual: Right panel draws a smooth white damped curve (labelled 'dish blot average', schematic) that rises once and fades. Then the left panel highlights individual living cells blinking teal one by one, and the right panel reveals crisp teal single-cell pulse traces of uniform height and width; turning up a coral 'gamma dose' slider adds extra pulses (1, then 2, then 3) without raising their peak height.
scenes.narration: Grind millions of irradiated cells onto a blot, and p53 rises and fades, at most with a ripple. That dish average looks like a dial. Film single living cells instead, and p53 fires separate pulses of fixed average height and width. Higher doses add more pulses on average, not taller ones.

scenes.tts: Why did the blot hide those pulses? Because cells pulse out of step. An average equals the sum divided by the cell count. Suppose four cells each peak at eighty, one after another. At any hour, eighty plus zero plus zero plus zero, divided by four, equals twenty. Out-of-step flashes blend into a low, smooth wave.
scenes.caption: Why did the blot hide those pulses? Because cells pulse out of step. An average equals the sum divided by the cell count. Suppose four cells each peak at 80, one after another. At any hour, 80 plus 0 plus 0 plus 0, divided by 4, equals 20. Out-of-step flashes blend into a low, smooth wave.
scenes.visual: Left panel stacks four individual cells (Cells 1 to 4) flashing bright teal sequentially in four time slots (computed example, labelled 'schematic units'). Right panel displays 'average = sum ÷ cell count' (size 28, white) above four staggered teal spikes of height 80; as a vertical time cursor sweeps across each slot, '(80 + 0 + 0 + 0) ÷ 4 = 20' builds live and traces a flat white average line across the graph at height 20.
scenes.narration: Why did the blot hide those pulses? Because cells pulse out of step. An average equals the sum divided by the cell count. Suppose four cells each peak at 80, one after another. At any hour, 80 plus 0 plus 0 plus 0, divided by 4, equals 20. Out-of-step flashes blend into a low, smooth wave.

scenes.tts: Those pulses follow gamma rays that break both strands. Do cells actually read that pulsing shape over time? Researchers blocked M D M two with a drug to hold p fifty-three steady at about one pulse's height. Same protein, same peak, only the shape differs. Will the steady cells still recover?
scenes.caption: Those pulses follow gamma rays that break both strands. Do cells actually read that pulsing shape over time? Researchers blocked MDM2 with a drug to hold p53 steady at about one pulse's height. Same protein, same peak, only the shape differs. Will the steady cells still recover?
scenes.visual: Right panel splits cleanly into two computed traces of equal peak height (schematic): top trace shows three separated teal pulses ('pulsed p53'); bottom trace shows an amber MDM2 blocker icon holding p53 flat in one continuous plateau at the same height ('steady p53'). Question card appears at top: 'Same peak, different shape: will steady cells still recover?'
scenes.narration: Those pulses follow gamma rays that break both strands. Do cells actually read that pulsing shape over time? Researchers blocked MDM2 with a drug to hold p53 steady at about one pulse's height. Same protein, same peak, only the shape differs. Will the steady cells still recover?

scenes.visual: Question card stays clear at top while the pulsed and steady teal traces of equal peak height sit side by side, the fate bar below hovers between teal 'Recover' and coral 'Permanent arrest', and a 4.5-second progress bar fills along the bottom.

scenes.tts: Mostly not, which means shape over time steered fate, not peak height alone. In the cell line studied, pulsing cells tended to recover and divide. Steady cells more often entered senescence, a permanent exit from division. Steady p fifty-three also meant more in total, yet at equal totals it still drove senescence genes harder. How a stress signal unfolds over time helps decide cell fate.

scenes.visual: Question card fades. Beside the pulsed trace, the fate bar fills bright teal ('recover and divide') and a left-panel cell divides cleanly into two. Beside the steady plateau trace, the fate bar shifts to coral ('senescence: permanent exit') and the cell locks in place with a coral ring.

scenes.tts: A similar brief-versus-lasting choice happens inside the endoplasmic reticulum, where secreted proteins fold with chaperone helpers. When unfolded chains pile up, three membrane sensors wake up, partly because the chaperone BiP leaves to bind the unfolded chains. First they buy time for repair by slowing new protein entry and ordering more chaperones.

scenes.visual: The left cell zooms smoothly onto a horizontal slate endoplasmic reticulum membrane carrying three teal sensor blocks (labelled 'IRE1', 'PERK', 'ATF6', schematic) capped by amber BiP chaperone blocks. Tangled coral unfolded chains accumulate inside the compartment, pulling amber BiP away so the three sensors light up. On the right, a short stress bar keeps the fate bar in teal ('repair: lower load, add chaperones').

scenes.tts: If that folding backlog drags on, those same sensors shift their message toward cell death. One branch activates a death-promoting factor called chop, while another signals through the stress kinase J N K. Stress strength and cell state matter too, and repair and death signals can overlap.
scenes.caption: If that folding backlog drags on, those same sensors shift their message toward cell death. One branch activates a death-promoting factor called CHOP, while another signals through the stress kinase JNK. Stress strength and cell state matter too, and repair and death signals can overlap.
scenes.visual: On the right time axis, the coral unfolded-protein stress bar extends longer; the fate bar blends gradually from teal repair into coral death (showing an explicit shaded overlap zone labelled 'strength & cell state matter'). From the PERK block a coral arrow lights up 'CHOP', and from the IRE1 block a coral arrow lights up 'JNK'.
scenes.narration: If that folding backlog drags on, those same sensors shift their message toward cell death. One branch activates a death-promoting factor called CHOP, while another signals through the stress kinase JNK. Stress strength and cell state matter too, and repair and death signals can overlap.

scenes.tts: Across both pathways, brief or pulsed signals favour repair, while sustained ones suggest repair is failing. One snapshot of protein level misses half the story. Reading the full timeline helps steer the cell between recovery and irreversible fate.

scenes.visual: Clean summary pairing on the same time axis: left half shows a brief or pulsed teal trace pointing to teal 'Repair & recover'; right half shows a sustained or prolonged trace shifting to coral 'Permanent arrest or death', with both panels fading smoothly into the end card.
scenes.narration: Across both pathways, brief or pulsed signals favour repair, while sustained ones suggest repair is failing. One snapshot of protein level misses half the story. Reading the full timeline helps steer the cell between recovery and irreversible fate.
